Series::threshold¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::threshold(double threshold_val, double value) const

Replacing A Lower Region¶

threshold() applies one scalar boundary independently to every lane:

$$ y_i = \begin{cases} x_i, & x_i > \text{threshold_val},\ \text{value}, & x_i \le \text{threshold_val}. \end{cases} $$

The strict > is the important detail. A lane exactly equal to the threshold is replaced. This makes the operation useful for hard activation floors, clipping a lower region to a sentinel, or constructing a piecewise constant branch without allocating a same-shaped condition Series.

The output has the receiver’s shape, dtype, and platform. Floating and signed or unsigned integral receivers are supported; Bool and complex receivers are rejected because an ordered numeric boundary is not meaningful for those families. Comparison uses the supplied floating threshold without first truncating it to an integral receiver’s dtype. The replacement is cast to the receiver dtype, so callers should choose a representable value.

Reverse Mode And Ownership¶

threshold() allocates a new Series and does not mutate the receiver. Its derivative with respect to each retained lane is one. Replaced lanes, including lanes exactly on the boundary, have derivative zero because their output is the constant value. The two scalar arguments are configuration values and do not receive sensitivity.

Use threshold_() only when deliberate mutation is required.

Examples¶

1. Observe the inclusive replacement boundary¶

const auto x = pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.threshold(0.5, -9.0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-9.0000, -9.0000, -9.0000, 1.0000]

The 0.5 lane is replaced because retention requires a value strictly greater than 0.5.

2. Compare integral lanes against a fractional boundary¶

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-1, 0, 1}).threshold(-0.5, 9.5));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[9, 0, 1]

The comparison remains against -0.5, so zero is retained. The replacement 9.5 is converted to the receiver’s int64 dtype and stored as 9.

3. Preserve higher-rank shape¶

const auto matrix = pluss::make_series({{-2.0, 0.0}, {2.0, 4.0}});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, matrix.threshold(1.0, 10.0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 10.0000 10.0000 ⎤
⎣  2.0000  4.0000 ⎦

Thresholding is elementwise; no axis is reduced or broadcast.

4. Inspect the piecewise reverse rule¶

auto tracked = x.clone();
tracked.tracks_slope_(true);
tracked.threshold(0.5, -9.0).sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, tracked.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000, 1.0000]

5. Reject an unordered receiver dtype¶

try {
  (void)pluss::make_series({true, false}).threshold(0.0, 1.0);
} catch (const std::exception& error) {
  std::cout << error.what() << '\n';
}

Output¶

threshold: bool input is not supported

See Also¶

  • threshold_() performs the same rule in place.

  • clamp_min() and clamp_max() impose one-sided numeric bounds.

  • where() selects between two general Series branches.
